## Speech language models as models of listening

In psycholinguistics research, surprisal is almost always computed from text, even in studies where people are listening to spoken input. We develop a framework to estimate it [directly from the audio]{.hl} with speech language models. Doing so raises questions about units: one word has many acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by a given speech LM. Using importance sampling, we marginalize over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model and study this estimated marginalized surprisal as a predictor of pupil dilation in listening studies.

*Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal* (to appear at EMNLP 2026).

## Getting the predictors right

Reading-time studies usually take contextual surprisal from a language model and word frequency from a separate corpus. We show how to [estimate both from the same model]{.hl}. We test whether downstream models of eye-tracking data in 11 languages change when unigram and contextual surprisal come from the same model.

::: {.feature}
### [Explore the unigram surprisal results](unigram/index.qmd)

Every model comparison from *Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics* (to appear at EMNLP 2026), across eleven MECO languages and three English corpora. Switch estimators, spillover, outlier removal, log-transformed reading times and multiple-comparison correction.

## Speech and text technology for language varieties

Dialect robustness in Catalan speech recognition, parallel data and a lemmatizer for the written varieties of Romansh, orthographic variation in Occitan, and low-resource speech translation. See [publications](publications.qmd).
